analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from forcing workers into arbitration and lets them sue or join class actions over workplace disputes.
analysis.headline: Introduced on July 30, 2026 by Rep. Jerrold Nadler with 7 Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the House Judiciary and Education and Workforce Committees, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit employers from requiring workers, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, to agree in advance to arbitrate workplace disputes or to give up the right to join group (class or collective) lawsuits. Arbitration would still be allowed after a dispute arises, but only if the worker agrees voluntarily, in writing, after at least a 45-day waiting period and with plain-language notice, and it would be illegal to retaliate against a worker who says no. The bill also defines "worker" to include independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled, and it would cover work disputes from wage claims to discrimination and wrongful discharge.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are bound by forced arbitration clauses — a large share of the private workforce, including low-wage, service, and gig workers — would regain the ability to take workplace disputes (wage theft, discrimination, harassment, wrongful discharge) to court and to join class or collective actions, which the bill's findings say is often the only affordable way to get relief. Workers who decline to arbitrate would gain protection against retaliation, with a right to sue and recover attorney's fees [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Bars pre-dispute arbitration agreements requiring arbitration of any work dispute, so workers keep the right to go to court.
Bans pre-dispute waivers of joint, class, or collective claims, restoring workers' ability to band together in group lawsuits.

Lets post-dispute arbitration proceed only if it is genuinely voluntary: not coerced or required as a condition of the job, explained in plain language, agreed to after a 45-day waiting period with the clock on the worker's claim paused, and confirmed in writing.
Makes it unlawful to retaliate against or threaten a worker who refuses to arbitrate, and gives the worker a private right to sue, with attorney's fees and costs, within two years (three if willful).
Amends the National Labor Relations Act to make requiring or enforcing such agreements an unfair labor practice, and voids any agreement that violates the rule; union-negotiated contracts are exempt.
Defines 'worker' to include independent contractors no matter what label the employer uses, and applies to the fullest extent the Constitution allows, including household and domestic workers.

Puts the decision on whether the law applies to an agreement and whether the agreement is valid in the hands of a court rather than the arbitrator, so the employer cannot steer the question to a privately chosen decision-maker.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use forced arbitration and class-action waivers would lose their ability to keep disputes out of court and to cap their exposure through individual arbitration; they would face more courtroom litigation and group suits, plus the legal and compliance cost of new rules on any post-dispute arbitration agreements. Arbitration firms would lose a large stream of employment-dispute business [S2].

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose the ability to resolve workplace disputes privately and quickly; every covered dispute could proceed to court, which typically costs more and takes longer to resolve than a single arbitration.

The bill applies to independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled and extends to household and domestic service work, so it reaches beyond large corporate workforces and could affect small household employers as well.

The bill is a direct response to Supreme Court rulings (including Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis) that enforced arbitration and class-action waivers; opponents argue Congress was changing course on settled law, which invites litigation over what the new rules mean.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is large and concrete: the bill's own findings state that forced individual dispute resolution leaves many workers seeking no redress at all, out of well-founded fear of retaliation, and that joining a group action is often the only affordable way to enforce their rights [S2]. Restoring court access would make wage theft, discrimination, and unlawful discharge claims enforceable in practice, not just on paper. The costs are real but mostly fall on employers, who would face more lawsuits, higher litigation costs, and the loss of private, predictable dispute resolution. The strongest good-faith objection is that individual arbitration is not always worse for a worker — it can be faster and cheaper than a lone court case — but the bill addresses this by leaving arbitration available after a dispute arises, with strict consent safeguards [S2]. A secondary concern is the bill's breadth: it reaches independent contractors and household/domestic employment, which will draw legal challenges and may sweep in small household employers alongside large corporations. On balance, the design is well targeted at the specific mechanism — pre-dispute coercion — rather than banning arbitration outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary and Education and Workforce Committees, where no vote or hearing has been taken; the bill is waiting and could still move before the Congress ends.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on July 30, 2026.
On introduction it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, additionally, to the House Education and Workforce Committee.
The full action history shows no hearing, markup, vote, or floor action after the referral.
As of the bill's Congress.gov page, the bill has not been reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on forced arbitration clauses benefit from the bill's inaction, because the status quo — workers funneled into individual arbitration and barred from group suits — remains fully in force. The bill's 8 sponsors have gained visibility with labor supporters but no policy result.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on July 30, 2026.

for.name: Rep. Robert Scott
for.role: Representative from Virginia, Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor alongside five other House Democrats when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill but has not scheduled a hearing or markup; no committee action is recorded in the bill's history.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the committees where the bill sits are controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.industry: Employers that require workers to sign arbitration and class-action waivers
industries.note: These companies would no longer be able to require arbitration and class-action waivers as a condition of work, meaning workplace claims could go to court and be litigated as group actions — higher litigation exposure and loss of a private, controlled dispute forum. Their interest in keeping the current system runs directly against workers' ability to enforce wage, discrimination, and discharge rights.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employment-dispute arbitration practices
industries.note: Arbitration of employment disputes would become available only after a dispute arises and with strict consent safeguards, shrinking the volume of employment arbitrations that today flow from pre-dispute clauses.

industries.industry: Gig-economy and platform companies that engage contractors
industries.note: Because the bill covers independent contractors regardless of their label, platform companies that use contractor arbitration clauses would be subject to the same rules as traditional employers.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority and no recorded committee action in the weeks since introduction, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; it will probably sit in committee until January 3, 2027 unless majority leadership decides otherwise. Its realistic path would be reintroduction in the next Congress, where its fate depends on which party controls the chamber.
